"The effects of the coronavirus will weigh on economic activity in the near term and pose risks to the economic outlook." That negative near-term assessment is clear, but the policy response described—cutting the federal funds rate to the effective lower bound, launching large-scale purchases of Treasuries and agency MBS, expanding repo operations, easing discount-window terms, and activating dollar swap lines—is consistent with the literature on monetary transmission through interest-rate and credit channels. Research on the bank-lending/credit channel (e.g., Kashyap, Lamont, and Stein; Gertler and Gilchrist) emphasizes that easing financial frictions lowers the external finance premium and supports investment and employment when private balance sheets are stressed. The use of balance-sheet tools and lender-of-last-resort facilities aligns with modern models of liquidity traps and credit market imperfections, in which central bank actions that stabilize funding markets can materially mitigate downturns. With market-based inflation compensation falling and inflation below 2 percent, the easing is also consistent with inflation-forecast targeting perspectives (Svensson) that stress anchoring expectations around the target to avoid deflationary spirals.

Netting these points, the tone remains cautious/negative due to imminent output and employment losses, but the literature-backed policy measures temper the downside compared with a pure-risk statement.
